patient.name: Robert Aldana
patient.chiefComplaint: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back

history.hpi: Patient was watching television when he developed sudden, severe 'tearing' chest pain that immediately radiated straight through to his upper back between the shoulder blades. Pain has remained constant at 10/10 since onset roughly 20 minutes ago, not positional, not reproducible with palpation. Denies exertion or trauma preceding the pain.
medications: Lisinopril 20 mg PO daily (admits frequent missed doses)
history.lastOralIntake: Dinner approximately 2 hours prior to symptom onset
history.events: Sudden onset while resting; wife called 911 immediately when he described the pain as 'ripping'

scene.dispatch: 65-year-old male, chest pain radiating to back, conscious and breathing, residence
scene.location: Single-family home living room, patient found seated in a recliner, leaning forward and clutching his chest
scene.bystanders: Wife present, witnessed sudden onset, called 911 immediately
visualCues: Patient pale, diaphoretic, visibly uncomfortable, guarding his chest
Leaning forward in the recliner, reluctant to move
Empty antihypertensive medication bottle visible on side table with several days' doses remaining unused

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 65-year-old male with sudden-onset severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back, pale and diaphoretic, with a markedly elevated and asymmetric blood pressure between arms.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking full sentences despite distress
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Right radial pulse bounding, left radial pulse notably weaker; skin pale, cool, diaphoretic
otherFindings: 10/10 tearing chest pain radiating straight through to the upper back
Blood pressure differs substantially between the right and left arms
Pain onset sudden and maximal at outset, not gradual
No chest wall tenderness to palpation
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "It feels like something's tearing inside my chest — it went straight through to my back."

transitions.if: Pulse/BP differential assessed and red flags recognized
transitions.condition: Crew obtains bilateral blood pressures and pulses, recognizes the asymmetry along with the sudden tearing chest-to-back pain as red flags for a possible aortic emergency, and proceeds with cautious management rather than treating as routine musculoskeletal pain.

phases.name: Pulse/BP differential assessed and red flags recognized
phases.description: Crew performs a full assessment including bilateral pulses and blood pressures, identifies the asymmetry and tearing chest-to-back pain as concerning for aortic dissection, provides cautious analgesia, and prepares for gentle transport to an appropriate specialty center.
phases.triggerCondition: After assessing bilateral pulses and blood pressures and finding a significant right-left differential in a patient with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, the crew recognizes this presentation as a possible life-threatening aortic emergency rather than routine chest or back pain.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Persistent right-left pulse and BP asymmetry confirmed on repeat exam; skin pale, cool, diaphoretic
otherFindings: Pain still 8/10 after initial analgesia, improved from 10/10
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "It still hurts, but a little less than before."

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess bilateral pulses and blood pressures for asymmetry; recognize as a red flag for aortic emergency
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Aortic dissection or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: Unequal femoral or distal lower extremity pulses. "Pulsatile" abdominal mass. Associated abdominal pain and/or chest pain. Known history of abdominal aortic aneurysm or dissection
expectedActions.rationale: Pulse or blood pressure asymmetry combined with tearing chest-to-back pain is a classic red flag for aortic dissection and changes destination and handling.

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain vascular access to allow analgesia administration
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Obtain vascular access as necessary to provide analgesia and/or fluid resuscitation
expectedActions.rationale: IV access is needed before administering parenteral analgesia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Fentanyl 85 mcg IV (85 kg x 1 mcg/kg = 85 mcg; max initial 100 mcg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For Moderate to Severe pain, analgesics include: Fentanyl: 1 mcg/kg IN, IM, IV or IO (maximum initial dose of 100 mcg)
expectedActions.rationale: Adequate analgesia reduces sympathetic surge and further blood pressure elevation, which is important in a suspected dissection.

expectedActions.shortAction: Position of comfort; minimize exertion and handle gently to avoid further BP spikes
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Non-pharmacologic pain management options include: Placement of the patient in a position of comfort. Verbal reassurance to control anxiety
expectedActions.rationale: Gentle handling and reduced anxiety help limit further hemodynamic stress on a potentially fragile aortic wall.

transitions.if: Specialty transport initiated with gentle handling
transitions.condition: With analgesia on board and red flags recognized, the crew transports gently and with minimal scene time to an appropriate specialty destination capable of managing a suspected aortic emergency.

Despite recognition and gentle handling, the patient develops sudden hypotension and tachycardia en route consistent with aortic rupture or tamponade, requiring shock management per the Shock Guideline.

phases.name: Specialty transport initiated with gentle handling
phases.description: Patient is packaged and transported gently to a facility capable of managing a suspected aortic emergency, with ongoing reassessment of pain, pulses, and vital signs throughout transport.
phases.triggerCondition: After analgesia and recognition of the aortic red flags, the patient is transported with minimized scene time, gentle handling, and continuous reassessment toward a specialty destination.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Persistent pulse/BP asymmetry, unchanged; skin remains pale and diaphoretic but no worsening
otherFindings: Reassessed vitals stable, no further BP escalation

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport to a specialty destination center for suspected aortic emergency; minimize scene time
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide transport to an appropriate receiving facility. Consider specialty destination centers for conditions such as suspected aortic emergency
expectedActions.rationale: Aortic dissection requires definitive surgical or specialty vascular care not available at all receiving facilities.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs and response to analgesia throughout transport
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Reassess vital signs and response to therapeutic interventions throughout transport
expectedActions.rationale: Ongoing reassessment detects early deterioration such as rupture or progression of the dissection.

phases.name: Deterioration into hypotension and shock
phases.description: The patient suddenly develops hypotension and worsening tachycardia en route, consistent with rupture or cardiac tamponade from the dissection. Crew must recognize and manage evolving shock per the Shock Guideline.
phases.triggerCondition: En route, the patient's blood pressure suddenly drops and heart rate rises with worsening pallor and diaphoresis, consistent with rupture or tamponade complicating the aortic dissection.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses now thready and difficult to palpate bilaterally; skin ashen, cool, diaphoretic
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact but patient increasingly lethargic
otherFindings: Sudden drop in blood pressure with rising heart rate
Patient now confused, slow to respond

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize shock and initiate treatment per the Shock Guideline; cautious fluids, prepare for rapid transport
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess for signs of shock. If shock is present, provide treatment per appropriate Shock Guideline
expectedActions.rationale: Sudden hypotension in a dissection patient suggests rupture or tamponade and is immediately life-threatening, requiring shock management and expedited transport.
